Most base rates are Free; the extra duty by country decides the cost: bullion exempt, Indian diamonds +10%, Israeli +12.5%, EU and Swiss diamonds Free.

overview.intro:
Chapter 71 covers pearls, diamonds and gemstones, lab-grown stones, gold, silver and the platinum-group metals in every form from doré to minted bars, precious-metal scrap, fine jewelry, silverware, costume jewelry and coin. **Most base rates are Free**: 73 of the 140 lines — every diamond, pearl, bullion, bar and coin line — pay nothing; fine jewelry pays 5%–13.5% and costume jewelry up to 11%.

The U.S. imported **$151.84B** of these goods in 2025, 74.1% more than in 2024, driven by precious metal: other precious-metal articles (7115.90, where minted bars are classified) $77.63B, gold $30.19B, platinum-group metals $10.29B and silver $8.45B. **Switzerland** ($59.04B) was the largest supplier, ahead of Australia, South Africa, Canada and Mexico; **India** ($6.57B) leads in diamonds and jewelry.

The extra duty depends on the product as much as on the country. **Bullion, bars, platinum-group metals and legal-tender coin are exempt** from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (note 52(b)) — they pay nothing from anywhere except China (25%, List 3). Diamonds, gemstones and jewelry pay the country rate: **+10% from India**, +12.5% from Israel, South Africa, Thailand and Hong Kong, 10% in total from the EU — but **EU and Swiss diamonds and gemstones are exempt**. China pays up to 31% on costume jewelry. Canadian polished diamonds, cast silver bars and jewelry pay a **50% Section 338 duty even under USMCA**, and Russian gold and diamonds cannot be imported.

productGroups.label: Pearls, natural or cultured (loose or temporarily strung)
productGroups.blurb: Natural and cultured pearls, loose or only temporarily strung for transport, are Free. Strung or set pearls are articles of heading 7116 or jewelry of 7113. Natural pearls from the EU and Switzerland are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty; cultured pearls are not.

productGroups.label: Diamonds, unmounted — rough, polished and industrial
productGroups.blurb: Every diamond line is Free — rough, polished (7102.39, split at 0.5 carat) and industrial. Rough diamonds (7102.10, 7102.21, 7102.31) need a Kimberley Process certificate. Russian-origin diamonds, and Russian-mined stones of 0.5 carat or more cut elsewhere, are banned. The extra duty differs by country: Free from Belgium and the rest of the EU, +10% from India, +12.5% from Israel and the UAE, 50% from Canada (Section 338).

productGroups.label: Rubies, sapphires, emeralds & other gemstones (unmounted)
productGroups.blurb: Rubies, sapphires, emeralds and other natural gemstones are Free, unworked or cut for jewelry; stones only sawn or roughly shaped (7103.10.40) and other worked stones (7103.99.50) pay 10.5%. EU and Swiss stones are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty.

productGroups.label: Lab-grown diamonds & other synthetic stones
productGroups.blurb: Lab-grown (synthetic) diamonds cut but not set and suitable for jewelry (7104.91.10) are Free; rough lab-grown diamonds (7104.21) pay 3%, other worked lab-grown diamonds 6.4%. Lab-grown stones are on no Section 301 exception list, so EU and Swiss goods pay the duty too.

productGroups.label: Diamond and gemstone dust & powder
productGroups.blurb: Natural and synthetic diamond dust and powder (abrasives) and other gemstone powder are Free.

productGroups.label: Silver — bullion, doré, bars, powder
productGroups.blurb: Silver bullion and doré and cast silver bars of 99.5% or more (7106.92.10) are Free; other unwrought and semi-manufactured silver 3%. Only unwrought bullion and doré (7106.91.10) is exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty, and Canadian silver bars are on the 50% Section 338 list.

productGroups.label: Base metals clad with silver
productGroups.blurb: Base metal clad with silver, not further worked than semi-manufactured: 3.3%.

productGroups.label: Gold — bullion, doré, bars, powder, leaf, monetary gold
productGroups.blurb: Gold bullion and doré (7108.12.10), gold bars of 99.5% or more marked only with weight and purity (7108.13.55), gold leaf, powder and monetary gold are Free; other unwrought and semi-manufactured gold 4.1%. Every 7108 line is exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty, but Chinese gold still pays the 25% List 3 duty.

productGroups.label: Base metals or silver clad with gold
productGroups.blurb: Base metal or silver clad with gold (gold-filled stock), not further worked than semi-manufactured: 6%.

productGroups.label: Platinum, palladium, rhodium, iridium, osmium & ruthenium
productGroups.blurb: Platinum, palladium, rhodium, iridium, osmium and ruthenium — unwrought, powder or semi-manufactured — are Free and exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty.

productGroups.label: Metals clad with platinum
productGroups.blurb: Base metals, silver or gold clad with platinum, not further worked than semi-manufactured: 10%.

productGroups.label: Precious-metal waste, scrap & ash
productGroups.blurb: Waste, scrap and ash of gold, silver and platinum metals for refining are Free. Platinum scrap and precious-metal ash are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty; gold and silver scrap are not.

productGroups.label: Jewelry of gold, silver, platinum or clad metal
productGroups.blurb: Fine jewelry pays 5%–13.5%: gold, platinum or other precious-metal rings, earrings, necklaces and bracelets mostly 5.5% (rope necklaces 5%, mixed-link 5.8%, chain by the length 7%); silver jewelry 5% (13.5% if valued not over $18 a dozen, 6.3% for chain); gold-clad jewelry 5.2%–7%.

productGroups.label: Silverware & goldsmiths' wares (tableware, flatware)
productGroups.blurb: Silversmiths' and goldsmiths' wares: knives with silver handles 2.8%, forks 2.7%, spoons 3.3%–3.5%, sterling tableware 3.3%, other silver articles 3%, articles of other precious metal 7.9%, of clad metal 3%.

productGroups.label: Other precious-metal articles — minted bars, platinum gauze
productGroups.blurb: Minted bars and rounds of 99.5% gold, silver or other precious metal marked only with weight and purity (7115.90.05) are Free and exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty; platinum catalyst gauze 4%, other gold articles 3.9%, silver 3%, others 4%.

productGroups.label: Articles of pearls & gemstones (strands, gemstone jewelry, carvings)
productGroups.blurb: Articles of pearls and gemstones: strands of natural pearls 3.3%, cultured pearls 5.5%; jewelry of precious or semiprecious stones 3.3% (not over $40 a piece) or 6.5%; graded semiprecious beads strung for transport 2.1%, figurines 4.5%, other 10.5%.

productGroups.label: Imitation (costume) jewelry
productGroups.blurb: Costume jewelry of base metal pays up to 11% (cuff links 8%, chain by the length 8% or 11%, other 11%); of plastics, glass and other materials 7.2% or 11%; religious articles 3.3%–3.9%; toy jewelry valued not over 8 cents a piece Free.

productGroups.label: Coins — bullion coins and other coin
productGroups.blurb: Coin is Free: gold bullion coins such as the Canadian Maple Leaf (7118.90) and other legal-tender coin are also exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty. Coin that is not legal tender (7118.10) is not, and from Canada it is on the 50% Section 338 list.

workedExamples.title: Polished diamond from India (over 0.5 carat)
workedExamples.body: The base rate is Free. India pays +10% under the 2026 Section 301 action (9903.05.44) and has no exception list, so a $100,000 parcel pays **$10,000**. The same stones cut in Belgium or Switzerland pay nothing (note 52(j), 9903.05.97/.98); from Israel or the UAE they pay 12.5%; from Canada 50% even under USMCA (Section 338). Between August 27, 2025 and February 6, 2026 the Indian parcel paid 50% under IEEPA. A stone of 0.5 carat or more mined in Russia cannot be imported at all.

workedExamples.title: Kilobar of gold from Switzerland
workedExamples.body: Cast and stamped 1-kilogram and 100-ounce bars are semi-manufactured gold, not unwrought bullion (CBP ruling NY N351466), and the base rate is Free. Every 7108 line is on the Section 301 general exemption list (note 52(b), 9903.05.86), so a $1,000,000 shipment pays **$0** — from Switzerland, the UK, Canada or anywhere else except China, where the 25% List 3 duty still applies. From August 7 to September 7, 2025 Swiss bars paid the 39% reciprocal duty.

workedExamples.title: 18-karat gold ring from Italy
workedExamples.body: The base rate is 5.5%. EU goods with a base rate under 10% pay 10% in total (9903.05.39), so a $50,000 order pays **$5,000**. The same ring pays 15.5% from India, 18% from the UAE, Thailand or Hong Kong, 12.5% from Israel under the FTA, 25.5% from China (5.5% + 12.5% + 7.5% List 4A) and 50% from Canada even under USMCA. If it is set with diamonds, the setting does not change the line: diamond jewelry of gold is still 7113.19.50.

workedExamples.title: Silver bars from Canada — cast or minted
workedExamples.body: Cast silver bars of 99.5% (7106.92.10, NY N357226) are Free, but the line is on the Canada Section 338 list, so they pay **50%** — $15,000 on $30,000 — even under USMCA, and 60% without a USMCA claim. Silver bullion and doré (7106.91.10), minted silver bars of 7115.90.05 and Canadian Maple Leaf coins (7118.90) are on neither the Section 338 list nor the Section 301 list, and enter Free. The line follows how the bar was made, not how it is sold.

workedExamples.title: Costume jewelry from China
workedExamples.body: Base-metal costume jewelry pays 11%. China adds +12.5% (9903.05.31) and +7.5% because the line is on List 4A (9903.88.15): **31%**, $3,100 on a $10,000 order. The same goods pay 21% from India, 23.5% from Thailand or Hong Kong and 11% from the EU (the base rate is already above 10%, so nothing is added). Since August 29, 2025 low-value parcels no longer enter duty-free under de minimis.

notes.chapterNotes:
**Note 1.** Subject to note 1(a) to section VI and except as provided below, all articles consisting wholly or partly: (a) of natural or cultured pearls or of precious or semiprecious stones (natural, synthetic or reconstructed), or (b) of precious metal or of metal clad with precious metal, are to be classified in this chapter.

**Note 2.** (a) Headings 7113, 7114 and 7115 do not cover articles in which precious metal or metal clad with precious metal is present as minor constituents only, such as minor fittings or minor ornamentation (for example, monograms, ferrules and rims), and paragraph (b) of the foregoing note does not apply to such articles. (b) Heading 7116 does not cover articles containing precious metal or metal clad with precious metal (other than as minor constituents).

**Note 3.** This chapter does not cover: (a) amalgams of precious metal or colloidal precious metal (heading 2843); (b) sterile surgical suture materials, dental fillings or other goods of chapter 30; (c) goods of chapter 32 (for example, lustres); (d) supported catalysts (heading 3815); (e) articles of heading 4202 or 4203 referred to in note 3(B) to chapter 42; (f) articles of heading 4303 or 4304; (g) goods of section XI (textiles and textile articles); (h) footwear, headgear or other articles of chapter 64 or 65; (ij) umbrellas, walking-sticks or other articles of chapter 66; (k) abrasive goods of heading 6804 or 6805 or chapter 82, containing dust or powder of precious or semiprecious stones (natural or synthetic); articles of chapter 82 with a working part of precious or semiprecious stones (natural, synthetic or reconstructed); machinery, mechanical appliances or electrical goods, or parts thereof, of section XVI. However, articles and parts thereof, wholly of precious or semiprecious stones (natural, synthetic or reconstructed) remain classified in this chapter, except unmounted worked sapphires and diamonds for styli (heading 8522); (l) articles of chapter 90, 91 or 92 (scientific instruments, clocks and watches, musical instruments); (m) arms or parts thereof (chapter 93); (n) articles covered by note 2 to chapter 95; (o) articles classified in chapter 96 by virtue of note 4 to that chapter; or (p) original sculptures or statuary (heading 9703), collectors' pieces (heading 9705) or antiques of an age exceeding one hundred years (heading 9706), other than natural or cultured pearls or precious or semiprecious stones.

**Note 4.** (a) The expression "precious metal" means silver, gold and platinum. (b) The expression "platinum" means platinum, iridium, osmium, palladium, rhodium and ruthenium. (c) The expression "precious or semiprecious stones" does not include any of the substances specified in note 2(b) to chapter 96.

**Note 5.** For the purposes of this chapter, any alloy (including a sintered mixture and an inter-metallic compound) containing precious metal is to be treated as an alloy of precious metal if any one precious metal constitutes as much as 2 percent, by weight, of the alloy. Alloys of precious metal are to be classified according to the following rules: (a) an alloy containing 2 percent or more, by weight, of platinum is to be treated as an alloy of platinum; (b) an alloy containing 2 percent or more, by weight, of gold but no platinum, or less than 2 percent, by weight, of platinum, is to be treated as an alloy of gold; (c) other alloys containing 2 percent or more, by weight, of silver are to be treated as alloys of silver.

**Note 6.** Except where the context otherwise requires, any reference in the tariff schedule to precious metal or to any particular precious metal includes a reference to alloys treated as alloys of precious metal or of the particular metal in accordance with the rules in note 5 above, but not to metal clad with precious metal or to base metal or non-metals plated with precious metal.

**Note 7.** Throughout the tariff schedule the expression "metal clad with precious metal" means material made with a base of metal upon one or more surfaces of which there is affixed by soldering, brazing, welding, hot-rolling or similar mechanical means a covering of precious metal. Except where the context otherwise requires, the expression also covers base metal inlaid with precious metal.

**Note 8.** Subject to note 1(a) to section VI, goods answering to a description in heading 7112 are to be classified in that heading and in no other heading of the tariff schedule.

**Note 9.** For the purposes of heading 7113, the expression "articles of jewelry" means: (a) any small objects of personal adornment (for example, rings, bracelets, necklaces, brooches, earrings, watch chains, fobs, pendants, tie pins, cuff links, dress studs, religious or other medals and insignia); and (b) articles of personal use of a kind normally carried in the pocket, in the handbag or on the person (for example, cigar or cigarette cases, snuff boxes, cachou or pill boxes, powder boxes, chain purses or prayer beads). These articles may be combined or set, for example, with natural or cultured pearls, precious or semiprecious stones, synthetic or reconstructed precious or semiprecious stones, tortoise shell, mother-of-pearl, ivory, natural or reconstituted amber, jet or coral.

**Note 10.** For the purposes of heading 7114, the expression "articles of goldsmiths' or silversmiths' wares" includes such articles as ornaments, tableware, toilet-ware, smokers' articles and other articles of household, office or religious use.

**Note 11.** For the purposes of heading 7117, the expression "imitation jewelry" means articles of jewelry within the meaning of paragraph (a) of note 9 above (but not including buttons or other articles of heading 9606, or dress combs, hair slides or the like, or hairpins, of heading 9615), not incorporating natural or cultured pearls, precious or semiprecious stones (natural, synthetic or reconstructed) nor (except as plating or as minor constituents) precious metal or metal clad with precious metal.

**Subheading notes.** 1. For the purposes of subheadings 7106.10, 7108.11, 7110.11, 7110.21, 7110.31 and 7110.41, the expressions "powder" and "in powder form" mean products of which 90 percent or more by weight passes through a sieve having a mesh aperture of 0.5 mm. 2. Notwithstanding the provisions of note 4(b), for the purposes of subheadings 7110.11 and 7110.19, the expression "platinum" does not include iridium, osmium, palladium, rhodium or ruthenium. 3. For the classification of alloys in the subheadings of heading 7110, each alloy is to be classified with that metal, platinum, palladium, rhodium, iridium, osmium or ruthenium, which predominates by weight over each other of these metals.

seo.shortDescription: What changed for HTS Chapter 71 — gold, silver, platinum, diamonds, gemstones, jewelry and coins — since January 2025: bullion exempt throughout, the end of the IEEPA duties (India 50%, Switzerland 39%), the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (India +10%, Israel +12.5%, EU diamonds exempt), Canada Section 338 and the Russian diamond bans, with Federal Register citations.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026). **No Chapter 71 base rate changed** — diamonds, gemstones, pearls and bullion stay Free, fine jewelry 5%–13.5%, costume jewelry up to 11%.

Everything that changed sits on top of the base rate. **Gold, silver and platinum bullion stayed exempt** from every 2025–2026 tariff: the reciprocal tariff exempted bullion from April 5, 2025 and cast gold bars from September 8, 2025, and the Section 122 surcharge and the 2026 Section 301 tariffs exempt the same 21 subheadings. **Diamonds and jewelry did not**: Indian diamonds and jewelry paid 25% from August 7, 2025 and 50% from August 27, Swiss goods 39%, South African 30%. The IEEPA duties **ended on February 24, 2026**, and the 10% Section 122 surcharge that replaced them expired on July 23, 2026. Since **July 24, 2026** a **Section 301 tariff** applies by country: India +10%, Israel, the UAE, South Africa, Thailand and Hong Kong +12.5%, EU goods 10% in total — with EU and Swiss diamonds, gemstones and natural pearls exempt. China still pays the List 3 (25%) or List 4A (7.5%) duty. Since **August 22, 2026** Canadian polished diamonds, silver bars, jewelry and some coin pay **50% under Section 338**, even under USMCA. Imports of Russian gold and diamonds remain banned.
tariffUpdates.scope: Measures that reach Chapter 71 from any country: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies and their exemption lists, the Brazil Section 301 tariff, the China Section 301 List 3 and List 4A duties, the Canada Section 338 duties, Russia's column 2 and 35% rates, and the 2025–2026 IEEPA and Section 122 duties that have ended. The OFAC import bans on Russian gold and diamonds, the Kimberley Process rules for rough diamonds, the de minimis suspension and preference-program changes (GSP, AGOA) are listed for reference. No Section 232 duty and no antidumping or countervailing duty order covers a Chapter 71 product. For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

Today Nicaragua pays the 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty (9903.05.58), which spares the bullion subheadings of note 52(b).

changes.title: Swiss rate cut to 15% in total; Swiss diamonds, gems and platinum exempt
changes.detail: Under the U.S.–Switzerland–Liechtenstein framework, Swiss goods paid 15% in total instead of the 39% reciprocal duty, and Swiss natural pearls, diamonds, gemstones, platinum-group metals, platinum scrap and coin were exempt (9903.02.84). Gold bars had been exempt since September 8. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: China fentanyl duty cut to 10%
changes.detail: The IEEPA duty on products of China and Hong Kong (9903.01.24) fell from +20% to +10%. It ended with the other IEEPA duties on February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Gold bars and other gold forms exempted from the reciprocal tariff
changes.detail: Executive Order 14346 replaced Annex II of the reciprocal-tariff order. From September 8, 2025 the exemption (9903.01.32) covered every gold line of 7108 — including cast bars of 7108.13.55, which CBP had ruled in July were not exempt — plus minted bars (7115.90.05) and other gold articles (7115.90.30), on top of the silver and gold bullion and doré, platinum-group metals, platinum scrap and legal-tender coin exempt since April 5. Ended with the reciprocal tariff on February 24, 2026.

changes.title: EU diamonds, gemstones and platinum exempted
changes.detail: Under the U.S.–EU framework, EU natural pearls, diamonds (7102.10, .31, .39), gemstones (7103), platinum-group metals, platinum scrap and coin paid no reciprocal duty (9903.02.74), retroactive to September 1, 2025. Other EU goods kept paying 15% in total. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: De minimis suspended for all countries
changes.detail: Executive Order 14324 ended duty-free de minimis treatment for shipments of any value, origin or mode, so online orders of jewelry and costume jewelry under $800 became dutiable. Executive Order 14388 continued the suspension after the IEEPA ruling.
changes.before: Free under de minimis up to $800

changes.title: Extra 25% on products of India
changes.detail: Executive Order 14329 added 25% on Indian goods (9903.01.84), on top of the 25% reciprocal rate in force since August 7, 2025: 50% in all on Indian polished diamonds and lab-grown diamonds, and 55.5% on gold jewelry (5.5% + 50%). Ended February 7, 2026.

changes.title: Country reciprocal rates replace the 10% baseline
changes.detail: Executive Order 14326 set country rates for goods entered from August 7, 2025: Switzerland +39%, South Africa +30%, India +25%, Thailand +19%, Israel +15%, the UAE, the UK, Australia, Peru and Colombia +10%; EU goods paid 15% in total. Diamonds and gemstones were not exempt; silver and gold bullion and doré, platinum-group metals and legal-tender coin were (Annex II). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional 40% on products of Brazil
changes.detail: Executive Order 14323 added 40% on Brazilian goods (9903.01.77) on top of the 10% reciprocal rate; silver and gold bullion and doré (7106.91.10, 7108.12.10) were exempt (9903.01.81), Brazilian gemstones and jewelry were not. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: CBP: cast 1-kilogram and 100-ounce gold bars are 7108.13.55, not exempt bullion
changes.detail: Ruling NY N351466 classified Swiss cast gold bars stamped with the refiner's logo, weight and fineness as semi-manufactured gold (7108.13.55), not unwrought bullion (7108.12.10), because stamping and lasering go beyond the "simple trimming" allowed by additional U.S. note 1(a). The bars were therefore subject to the reciprocal tariff — 39% for Switzerland from August 7 — until Executive Order 14346 exempted them from September 8, 2025.

changes.title: Canada additional duty raised to 35%
changes.detail: Raised the IEEPA duty on non-USMCA Canadian goods to +35% (9903.01.10). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: China reciprocal duty cut from 125% to 10%
changes.detail: Executive Order 14298 cut the reciprocal duty on Chinese goods to 10% for goods entered from May 14, 2025. Chinese costume jewelry (11% base) then paid 11% + 7.5% (List 4A) + 20% + 10% = 48.5% until November 9, 2025. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: China reciprocal duty raised to 125%
changes.detail: Executive Order 14266 raised the reciprocal duty on Chinese goods to 125% from April 10, 2025. With the 20% fentanyl duty and the 7.5% List 4A duty, Chinese costume jewelry paid 163.5% until May 13, 2025. Bullion on Annex II stayed exempt from the reciprocal duty.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff on products of all countries — bullion exempt
changes.detail: 10% baseline (9903.01.25) from April 5, 2025, and country rates (9903.02.xx); Canada and Mexico excluded. Annex II (9903.01.32) exempted silver bullion and doré (7106.91.10), gold bullion and doré (7108.12.10), the platinum-group metals of 7110, platinum scrap (7112.92) and legal-tender coin (7118.90) — but not cast gold bars (7108.13) or minted bars (7115.90.05) until September 8. Diamonds, gemstones and jewelry were not exempt. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Kimberley Process participant list updated
changes.detail: The State Department republished the list of Kimberley Process participants from which rough diamonds (7102.10, 7102.21, 7102.31) may be imported under the Clean Diamond Trade Act, adding Uzbekistan. Rough diamonds from a non-participant cannot be imported.

changes.title: China fentanyl duty raised to 20%
changes.detail: The IEEPA duty on products of China and Hong Kong (9903.01.20, then 9903.01.24) went from +10% (from February 4, 2025) to +20%, on top of the List 3 and List 4A duties. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Mexico
changes.detail: +25% on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.01) from March 4, 2025; USMCA-qualifying goods exempt from March 7. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Canada
changes.detail: +25% on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.10) from March 4, 2025, later raised to +35%; USMCA-qualifying goods exempt from March 7. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Ban on Russian-mined diamonds cut elsewhere extended to 0.5 carat
changes.detail: The second phase of OFAC's February 8, 2024 determination: non-industrial diamonds of 0.5 carat or more that were mined in Russia cannot be imported even after cutting and polishing in India, Belgium or elsewhere. General License 104B allows stones that were outside Russia before the cut-off dates through September 1, 2027.

changes.title: Ban on Russian diamond jewelry and on Russian-mined diamonds of 1 carat or more
changes.detail: OFAC determinations under E.O. 14068, as amended by E.O. 14114, banned imports of diamond jewelry and unsorted diamonds of Russian origin or exported from Russia, and of Russian-mined non-industrial diamonds of 1.0 carat or more even after they are transformed in another country.

changes.title: Russia: 35% on more precious-metal lines
changes.detail: Proclamation 10523 added platinum, semi-manufactured palladium, rhodium, iridium, osmium and ruthenium (7110) and industrial diamonds (7102.21.30, .40, 7102.29) to the 35% rate in place of column 2 (9903.90.08, note 30(b)).

changes.title: Russia: 35% in place of column 2 on diamonds, silver, gold bars and coin
changes.detail: Proclamation 10420 set 35% (9903.90.08) on Russian miners' diamonds, gemstones, synthetic and lab-grown stones, diamond and gemstone dust, silver bullion and bars, gold bars, minted bars and coin, among other products.

changes.title: Import ban on Russian gold
changes.detail: OFAC determined that the E.O. 14068 import prohibition applies to gold of Russian Federation origin, except gold that was outside Russia before June 28, 2022.

changes.title: Russia and Belarus moved to column 2 rates
changes.detail: The Suspending Normal Trade Relations with Russia and Belarus Act applied column 2 rates to their goods — from Free to 110% in Chapter 71 (for example 80% on gold jewelry, 110% on costume jewelry).

changes.title: Import ban on Russian non-industrial diamonds
changes.detail: Executive Order 14068 prohibited imports of non-industrial diamonds of Russian Federation origin (along with seafood and alcoholic beverages).

changes.title: China List 4A duty cut to 7.5%
changes.detail: USTR halved the List 4A duty (9903.88.15) from 15% to 7.5% under the Phase One agreement. It still applies to Chinese pearls, diamonds, gemstones, lab-grown stones, jewelry, costume jewelry and coin.

changes.title: China List 4A reaches jewelry, diamonds and pearls
changes.detail: The fourth China Section 301 list put +15% on Chinese pearls, diamonds, gemstones, synthetic stones, jewelry, costume jewelry and coin (headings 7101–7104, 7113, 7116–7118).

changes.title: China List 3 duty raised to 25%
changes.detail: USTR raised the List 3 duty (9903.88.03) from 10% to 25%. It covers Chinese gold, silver, platinum-group metals, precious-metal scrap, silverware and other precious-metal articles (7105–7112, 7114, 7115) and industrial diamonds (7102.21, 7102.29).

changes.title: China Section 301 List 3 reaches precious metals
changes.detail: The third China Section 301 list put +10% on Chinese precious metals, bullion, scrap, silverware and industrial diamonds.

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of Chapter 71 goods were **$151.84B in 2025**, 74.1% more than the $87.20B of 2024 and well above the $104.82B of 2020. Almost all of the jump was precious metal: other precious-metal articles (7115.90, which includes minted bars) rose from $21.23B to $77.63B, gold (7108) from $15.95B to $30.19B, silver from $5.09B to $8.45B and the platinum-group metals from $6.98B to $10.29B.

**Switzerland** supplied $59.04B (39%), four times its 2024 level — $49.45B in 7115 and $8.24B in gold. **Australia** ($12.69B) and **Canada** ($11.56B) ship gold and bars; **South Africa** ($11.83B) is the main source of platinum-group metals ($5.19B); **Mexico** ($7.79B) of silver ($4.01B).

Diamonds and jewelry fell. Diamond imports (7102) halved to $7.53B from $15.36B: India $3.47B, Israel $1.81B, Belgium $1.03B. **India** as a whole dropped 44.7% to $6.57B and **Israel** 53.9% to $2.00B. Fine jewelry (7113) was $12.06B, led by India ($2.19B), Italy ($1.88B), France ($1.71B) and Thailand ($1.35B); lab-grown and synthetic stones (7104) $602M, mostly from India; costume jewelry (7117) $808M, mostly from China.

The figures are annual and stop at 2025, before the 2026 tariff changes (the end of the IEEPA duties in February, the Section 301 tariffs from July 24, 2026 and the Canada Section 338 duties from August 22); they do not show what those changes did. Duty-collected figures are not available from an official source yet.

industryAreas.intro:
Most Chapter 71 base rates are Free, so the total a shipment pays is mostly the **extra duty for its country of origin**. Each cell below is the base rate for that product group plus the extra duty for that country, minus any preference — taken from the current tariff schedule.

**Bullion pays nothing from anywhere** except China: gold, silver bullion and doré, platinum-group metals, minted bars and legal-tender coin are on the Section 301 exemption list. For everything else the Section 301 tariff of July 24, 2026 applies: **+10% for India**, **+12.5% for Israel, the UAE, South Africa, Thailand and Hong Kong**, **10% in total for the EU** and **12.5% in total for Switzerland and Japan** — but **EU and Swiss diamonds, gemstones and natural pearls are exempt**, so Antwerp and Swiss stones enter Free while Indian ones pay 10%. China pays +12.5% plus 25% (List 3) or 7.5% (List 4A). USMCA-qualifying goods from Mexico pay nothing; from Canada, polished diamonds, cast silver bars, jewelry, costume jewelry and non-legal-tender coin pay **50% under Section 338** even with a USMCA claim.

tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 71: Gold, Diamonds, Jewelry & Precious Metals — Import Rules & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Gold, Diamonds & Jewelry into the U.S.: Kimberley Process, Russian Diamond Ban, Stamping Act & Legal Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 71) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What each HTS Chapter 71 line needs at U.S. entry — Kimberley Process certificates for rough diamonds, the OFAC bans on Russian gold and diamonds, origin marking, the Gold and Silver Stamping Act and FTC Jewelry Guides — and the legal ways to pay less: bullion versus bar classification, origin, USMCA, FTAs, repairs abroad, carnets, drawback and FTZs.
keywords: usmca hts chapter 71 rules of origin

tariffEngineering.intro:
Most Chapter 71 goods need no import license, but three rules stop shipments at the border. **Rough diamonds** need an original **Kimberley Process certificate**, a sealed tamper-resistant container and a participant country of export. **Russian gold and diamonds** are banned by OFAC — including Russian-mined diamonds of 0.5 carat or more that were cut in India, Belgium or elsewhere. And gold and silver articles stamped with a quality mark must meet it under the **National Gold and Silver Stamping Act**; every article must be marked with its country of origin.

On cost, the base rate is often Free, so the levers are mostly about the **extra duty**: whether metal is exempt bullion or a dutiable bar (cast silver bars are not exempt from the Section 301 duty, minted ones are), where a diamond was cut (Free from Belgium, +10% from India, 50% from Canada), USMCA and FTA claims, repairs abroad, carnets for show goods, drawback and foreign-trade zones. Each lever depends on a document, listed below with its regulation.

levers.title: Classify precious metal by its form — bullion, bar or "other"
levers.saves: Up to 4.1% of the value, and in some cases the whole Section 301 or Section 338 duty: unwrought gold bullion and doré (7108.12.10) and plain bars of 99.5% gold (7108.13.55) are Free, other unwrought or semi-manufactured gold 4.1%; silver bullion (7106.91.10) is exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty, cast silver bars (7106.92.10) are not, minted bars (7115.90.05) are
levers.appliesTo: Headings 7106, 7108, 7110 and 7115 — bullion, bars, grain, rounds and semi-manufactured precious metal
levers.document: Assay certificates showing fineness, and a description of how the bar was made (cast, minted, stamped, lasered) and what is marked on it.
levers.caveat: "Unwrought" excludes cast forms processed beyond simple trimming (additional U.S. note 1(a)), so CBP classified stamped and lasered 1-kilogram and 100-ounce cast gold bars in 7108.13.55 (NY N351466) and stamped cast silver bars in 7106.92.10 (NY N357226). The form follows the goods; a ruling settles a doubtful bar before it ships.

levers.title: Classify stones by how far they are worked — and natural or lab-grown
levers.saves: Up to 10.5%: unworked gemstones (7103.10.20) and stones cut for jewelry (7103.99.10) are Free, while stones only sawn or roughly shaped (7103.10.40) and other worked stones (7103.99.50) pay 10.5%; lab-grown diamonds cut for jewelry (7104.91.10) are Free, other worked lab-grown diamonds 6.4%
levers.appliesTo: Headings 7102–7104 — diamonds, gemstones and lab-grown stones
levers.document: Grading or laboratory reports stating whether a stone is natural or laboratory-grown, its weight and how it is cut.
levers.caveat: Only natural diamonds and gemstones are on the EU, Swiss and other note 52(j) exception lists; lab-grown diamonds pay the Section 301 duty from every country on the list. The FTC requires lab-grown diamonds to be disclosed as such (16 CFR 23.12).

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(j)

levers.title: Know the country of origin — where the stone was cut or the jewelry made
levers.saves: The difference between country rates: Free for EU and Swiss diamonds, +10% for Indian, +12.5% for Israeli, UAE or South African, 50% for Canadian polished diamonds; jewelry 10% in total from the EU, 15.5% from India, 18% from the UAE or Thailand, 25.5% from China
levers.appliesTo: All lines outside the bullion exemption; the gap is widest on diamonds and jewelry
levers.document: Production records showing where the stone was cut and polished, or where the jewelry was made; mine-of-origin records for diamonds of 0.5 carat or more.
levers.caveat: For duty, origin is where the goods were last substantially transformed. The OFAC Russia rules look further back: a diamond of 0.5 carat or more mined in Russia stays banned after it is cut in another country, so the supplier's mine-of-origin evidence matters.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 20, 51, 52

levers.title: Claim USMCA on Canadian and Mexican goods
levers.saves: The 10% Section 301 duty and the base rate (up to 13.5% on silver jewelry, 11% on costume jewelry)
levers.appliesTo: Goods of Canada and Mexico that meet the USMCA rules of origin
levers.document: A USMCA certification of origin (importer, exporter or producer) with the required data elements, and records supporting it.
levers.caveat: The claim does not remove the 50% Section 338 duty on the seven Canadian subheadings on the note 51(b)(3) list — polished diamonds, cast silver bars, silver and gold jewelry, costume jewelry and non-legal-tender coin. Bullion is exempt from Section 301 with or without a claim.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 51, 52

levers.title: Use an FTA or AGOA for the base rate
levers.saves: The base rate — 5%–13.5% on jewelry, 10.5% on worked gemstones — for goods of Israel, Australia, Peru, Colombia, Korea, other FTA partners and AGOA countries
levers.appliesTo: Dutiable lines with a Free special rate (most of 7103–7117)
levers.document: Proof that the goods meet the agreement's rules of origin: manufacturer affidavits, bills of materials, production and payment records.
levers.caveat: Under U.S. note 52(a) the 2026 Section 301 duty still applies when a special rate is claimed, so Israeli or South African jewelry pays 12.5% instead of 17.5%–18%. CBP denies claims it cannot verify; in HQ H307425 it denied a gold-jewelry FTA claim for lack of production and payment records. GSP has been expired since December 31, 2020.

citations.label: CBP ruling HQ H307425 (gold jewelry FTA claim)
HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(a)

levers.title: Repairs abroad and American goods returned
levers.saves: Duty on the full value: jewelry sent abroad for repair or alteration pays duty only on the value of the work (9802.00.40, 9802.00.50), and U.S.-made jewelry returned unchanged is Free (9801.00.10)
levers.appliesTo: U.S. goods exported and brought back — repairs, resizing, setting, returns from shows
levers.document: Export records, the foreign repairer's invoice for the work, and the declarations in 19 CFR 10.1 and 10.8.
levers.caveat: The Section 301 duty applies to the value of repairs or alterations under 9802 (note 52(a)). Assembly abroad of U.S. components (9802.00.80) does not cover U.S. gold that is melted and cast abroad — that is fabrication, not assembly (NY N347575).

levers.title: Bring show samples in under bond or an ATA Carnet
levers.saves: All duty on jewelry and stones shown at a trade show or to buyers and then re-exported
levers.appliesTo: Samples, exhibition pieces and consignments that leave the country again
levers.document: A temporary importation bond (9813.00.20 for samples for taking orders) or an ATA Carnet, and proof of export within the bond period.
levers.caveat: Goods properly entered under a Chapter 98 provision other than 9802 are outside the 2026 Section 301 duty (note 52(a)), but goods sold in the United States must be entered and pay full duty; the bond is forfeited if they are not exported in time.

levers.title: Claim drawback on re-exported goods
levers.saves: Up to 99% of the duties paid, including the Section 301 duty, on goods exported or destroyed
levers.appliesTo: Imported diamonds, gemstones, metal and jewelry that are re-exported, or used to make exported jewelry
levers.document: Import and export records linked by drawback claim, filed in ACE within five years of import.
levers.caveat: Drawback needs records tying each export to the import; substitution rules require goods of the same 8-digit subheading.

levers.title: Use a foreign-trade zone
levers.saves: Duty on goods re-exported from the zone, and deferral until goods enter U.S. commerce
levers.appliesTo: Stocks of stones, metal or jewelry held for distribution or re-export
levers.document: Zone admission (CBP Form 214) and an inventory-control system approved for the zone.
levers.caveat: Privileged foreign merchandise is classified at the rate in force on the date its privileged status is applied for; non-privileged merchandise is classified as it is when entered for consumption from the zone (19 CFR 146.65). Extra-duty notices can set their own zone-status rules, so check the current Chapter 99 note.

levers.title: Get a binding ruling
levers.saves: Certainty on the line — for example bullion versus bar, natural versus lab-grown, jewelry versus costume jewelry — and on the Chapter 99 numbers that go with it
levers.appliesTo: Any line where the form, the material or the value break is in doubt
levers.document: A ruling request with samples or photos, assay data and a full description.
levers.caveat: A ruling binds CBP only for goods that match the facts given.

rules.title: Rough diamonds (7102.10, 7102.21, 7102.31) may be imported only from a Kimberley Process participant, sealed in a tamper-resistant container and with an original Kimberley Process certificate, which the ultimate consignee keeps five years and sends to the Census Bureau

Imports of Russian-origin gold, non-industrial diamonds, unsorted diamonds and diamond jewelry are prohibited, and so are non-industrial diamonds of 0.5 carat or more mined in Russia and cut elsewhere (General License 104B allows stones that were outside Russia before the cut-off dates, through September 1, 2027)
Every article must be marked with its country of origin, or its container where the article cannot be; Native American-style jewelry must be marked indelibly on the article itself

rules.agency: National Gold and Silver Stamping Act
rules.title: Gold and silver articles stamped with a quality mark ("14K", "sterling") must meet it within the legal tolerances, and a quality mark must be accompanied by a registered trademark; importing falsely marked gold or silver ware is unlawful
The FTC Jewelry Guides govern how gold karat, silver ("sterling" = 925), platinum, diamonds, lab-grown diamonds, pearls, gemstone treatments and stone weights may be described when the goods are sold
Children's jewelry is a children's product: lead content must be within the statutory limit, and the importer must issue and eFile a Children's Product Certificate based on third-party testing
Circulating coin imported for monetary purposes needs no formal entry (additional U.S. note 2), but transporting more than $10,000 in coin or currency into the United States must be reported

Report the right Chapter 99 numbers with the Chapter 71 line: 9903.05.86 for the bullion exemption, 9903.05.97 or 9903.05.98 for EU or Swiss diamonds and gemstones, 9903.05.93/.94 for USMCA goods, 9903.03.14 for the Canada Section 338 list, 9903.88.03 or 9903.88.15 for China

groups.label: Pearls, natural or cultured (loose or temporarily strung)
groups.note: No license needed. Loose pearls are Free; natural pearls from the EU and Switzerland are also exempt from the Section 301 duty, cultured pearls from Japan pay 12.5% in total.

groups.label: Diamonds, unmounted — rough, polished and industrial
groups.note: Rough diamonds (7102.10, 7102.21, 7102.31) need a Kimberley Process certificate and must come from a participant. Russian-origin diamonds, and Russian-mined stones of 0.5 carat or more cut elsewhere, are banned. Canadian polished diamonds (7102.39) pay the 50% Section 338 duty even under USMCA.

groups.label: Rubies, sapphires, emeralds & other gemstones (unmounted)
groups.note: No license needed. Stones only sawn or roughly shaped, and worked stones not cut for jewelry, pay 10.5%; the rest are Free. EU, Swiss and some other countries' stones are exempt from the Section 301 duty (note 52(j)).

groups.label: Lab-grown diamonds & other synthetic stones
groups.note: Lab-grown diamonds must be sold as laboratory-grown (FTC). Russian-mined diamonds are covered by the OFAC ban only if natural. Cut lab-grown diamonds for jewelry are Free; lab-grown stones are on no Section 301 exception list.

groups.label: Diamond and gemstone dust & powder
Silver — bullion, doré, bars, powder
groups.note: Silver bullion and doré are exempt from the Section 301 duty; cast silver bars (7106.92.10) are not, and from Canada they pay the 50% Section 338 duty even under USMCA.

groups.label: Base metals clad with silver
groups.note: Silver-clad base metal pays 3.3%; no agency rule.

groups.label: Gold — bullion, doré, bars, powder, leaf, monetary gold
groups.note: Every gold line is exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty (note 52(b)); Chinese gold still pays the 25% List 3 duty. Russian gold is banned. Stamped cast bars are 7108.13.55, not unwrought bullion (NY N351466).

groups.label: Base metals or silver clad with gold
groups.note: Gold-clad base metal pays 6%; no agency rule.

groups.label: Platinum, palladium, rhodium, iridium, osmium & ruthenium
groups.note: Platinum-group metals are Free and exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty. Russian platinum-group metals pay column 2 or 35%.

groups.label: Metals clad with platinum
groups.note: Platinum-clad metal pays 10%; no agency rule.

groups.label: Precious-metal waste, scrap & ash
groups.note: Scrap for refining is Free; platinum scrap and ash are exempt from the Section 301 duty, gold and silver scrap are not.

groups.label: Jewelry of gold, silver, platinum or clad metal
groups.note: Gold and silver jewelry with a quality mark must meet it and carry a trademark (Stamping Act). Russian diamond jewelry is banned. Canadian silver and gold jewelry (7113.11.50, 7113.19.29, 7113.19.50) pay the 50% Section 338 duty.

groups.label: Silverware & goldsmiths' wares (tableware, flatware)
groups.note: Silverware with a "sterling" or karat mark must meet it (Stamping Act, FTC Guides). Base rates 2.7%–7.9%.

groups.label: Other precious-metal articles — minted bars, platinum gauze
groups.note: Minted bars of 99.5% metal (7115.90.05) are Free and exempt from the Section 301 duty; other gold articles (7115.90.30) are exempt too.

groups.label: Articles of pearls & gemstones (strands, gemstone jewelry, carvings)
groups.note: Pearl strands and gemstone jewelry pay 2.1%–10.5%; disclosures of pearl and gemstone treatments follow the FTC Guides.

groups.label: Imitation (costume) jewelry
groups.note: Costume jewelry for children needs lead testing and a Children's Product Certificate. Canadian base-metal costume jewelry (7117.19.90) pays the 50% Section 338 duty.

groups.label: Coins — bullion coins and other coin
groups.note: Circulating coin for monetary use needs no formal entry; coin and currency over $10,000 must be reported. Legal-tender coin is exempt from the Section 301 duty; non-legal-tender coin from Canada pays 50%.

faqs.question: Is gold exempt from U.S. tariffs?
searchedAs: is gold exempt from us tariffs
are gold and silver exempt from tariffs
faqs.answer: Yes, almost everywhere. Every gold line of heading 7108 — bullion, doré, cast bars, powder, leaf — plus minted bars (7115.90.05) and legal-tender coin (7118.90) has a Free base rate and is on the general exemption list of the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (note 52(b), 9903.05.86). They were also exempt from the 10% Section 122 surcharge (February 24 – July 23, 2026) and from the 2025 reciprocal tariff — unwrought bullion from April 5, 2025, cast bars only from September 8, 2025. The exception is China: Chinese gold still pays the 25% List 3 duty. Gold jewelry is not exempt (see below), and Russian gold cannot be imported.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on Swiss gold bars?
faqs.answer: Nothing today. Swiss 1-kilogram and 100-ounce cast bars are 7108.13.55 (Free) and exempt from the 12.5%-in-total Section 301 rate on Swiss goods. In 2025 they were not: CBP ruled on July 31, 2025 (NY N351466) that stamped cast bars are semi-manufactured gold, not exempt unwrought bullion, so they paid the 39% Swiss reciprocal rate from August 7 until Executive Order 14346 exempted all gold forms from September 8, 2025. Swiss gold jewelry pays 12.5% in total; Swiss diamonds and gemstones are exempt.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on gold jewelry from India to the USA?
searchedAs: tariff on gold jewelry from india to usa
tariff on gold from india to usa
tariff on jewelry from india to usa
faqs.answer: Indian gold jewelry (7113.19, mostly 5.5%) pays 15.5% — the base rate plus the 10% Section 301 duty on Indian goods (9903.05.44) in force since July 24, 2026. Silver jewelry pays 15%. GSP, which once made it duty-free, expired in 2020. In 2025 the same jewelry paid 30.5% from August 7 and 55.5% from August 27 under IEEPA; those duties ended in February 2026, and importers can claim refunds through CBP's CAPE process. Gold bars and bullion from India are exempt.

faqs.question: What is the U.S. tariff on diamonds from India?
searchedAs: tariff on diamonds from india to usa
tariff on loose diamonds from india to usa
faqs.answer: Cut and polished diamonds (7102.39) have a Free base rate. Since July 24, 2026 Indian diamonds pay the 10% Section 301 duty — $10,000 on a $100,000 parcel — because India has no exception list for stones. Lab-grown diamonds from India (7104.91.10) pay 10% too. The "50% tariff on diamonds" was the IEEPA rate on Indian goods from August 27, 2025; it fell to 25% on February 7, 2026 and ended on February 24, 2026.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on diamonds from Israel and Belgium?
searchedAs: import duty on diamonds in usa
faqs.answer: Israeli polished diamonds pay 12.5% (9903.05.47); the U.S.–Israel FTA does not remove the Section 301 duty. Diamonds from Belgium and every other EU country, and from Switzerland, enter Free: the EU and Swiss exception lists in note 52(j) cover unsorted, rough and polished non-industrial diamonds (7102.10, 7102.31, 7102.39). UAE and South African diamonds pay 12.5%, Canadian polished diamonds 50%.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on silver and silver bullion?
faqs.answer: Silver bullion and doré (7106.91.10) are Free and exempt from the Section 301 duty. Cast silver bars of 99.5% (7106.92.10) are Free but not exempt: they pay the country's Section 301 rate — 10% from the UK or Mexico (unless USMCA), 12.5% in total from Switzerland — and from Canada the 50% Section 338 duty, even under USMCA. Minted silver bars (7115.90.05) and legal-tender silver coins (7118.90) are exempt. Other semi-manufactured silver pays 3%.

faqs.question: What are the tariffs on jewelry from China?
searchedAs: tariffs on jewelry from china to usa
us tariff on jewelry from china
are there tariffs on jewelry from china
tariff on jewelry from china to usa
faqs.answer: Chinese jewelry pays the base rate plus 12.5% (2026 Section 301, 9903.05.31) plus 7.5% (List 4A, 9903.88.15): gold jewelry 25.5%, silver jewelry 25%, base-metal costume jewelry 31%. Toy jewelry and a few pearl and gemstone lines on the suspended List 4B pay only the 12.5%. Chinese gold and silver bullion pays 25% (List 3). USTR kept both lists after its 2026 review.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on jewelry from Canada, the UK, Italy and Australia?
searchedAs: tariff on jewelry from canada to usa
tariff on jewelry from uk to usa
tariff on jewelry from australia to usa
faqs.answer: Canada: silver and gold jewelry (7113.11.50, 7113.19.29, 7113.19.50) and base-metal costume jewelry (7117.19.90) pay 50% under Section 338 even when USMCA is claimed; other USMCA-qualifying jewelry pays nothing. UK: base rate + 10% — 15.5% on gold jewelry. Italy and the rest of the EU: 10% in total on gold and silver jewelry. Australia: the FTA removes the base rate, but the 12.5% Section 301 duty applies.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on lab-grown diamonds?
faqs.answer: Lab-grown diamonds are synthetic stones of heading 7104. Cut but unset lab-grown diamonds for jewelry (7104.91.10) are Free; rough ones (7104.21) pay 3%, other worked ones 6.4%. Unlike natural diamonds they are on no Section 301 exception list, so they pay the country rate from everywhere on the list — 10% from India, 20% from China (12.5% + 7.5%), 10% in total from the EU. They must be described as laboratory-grown when sold (16 CFR 23.12).

faqs.question: Why are Russian diamonds banned, and what does the ban cover?
faqs.answer: Under Executive Order 14068 (March 2022), the sanctions over Russia's war against Ukraine, imports of non-industrial diamonds of Russian origin are prohibited. Since March 1, 2024 the ban also covers Russian diamond jewelry and unsorted diamonds, and Russian-mined diamonds of 1.0 carat or more even if cut in another country — 0.5 carat or more since September 1, 2024. OFAC General License 104B lets stones that were outside Russia before those dates in through September 1, 2027. Russian gold has been banned since June 28, 2022.

faqs.question: What is the Kimberley Process, and how does it apply to U.S. imports?
faqs.answer: The Kimberley Process Certification Scheme tracks rough diamonds to keep conflict diamonds out of trade. Under the Clean Diamond Trade Act (19 U.S.C. 3903) and 31 CFR part 592, rough diamonds (7102.10, 7102.21, 7102.31) may be imported only from a participant listed by the State Department, sealed in a tamper-resistant container, with an original Kimberley Process certificate that the importer keeps five years. It does not apply to polished diamonds or jewelry and adds no duty.

faqs.question: What are the HS codes for jewelry, gold and diamonds?
searchedAs: hs code for jewelry sterling silver
hs code for gold plated jewelry
faqs.answer: Gold or platinum jewelry: 7113.19 (rings, earrings, bracelets mostly 7113.19.50, 5.5%); sterling silver jewelry: 7113.11 (5% for most); gold-plated or other costume jewelry: 7117 (up to 11%). Gold bullion and doré: 7108.12.10; cast gold bars: 7108.13.55; minted bars: 7115.90.05. Loose polished diamonds: 7102.39 (split at 0.5 carat); rough diamonds: 7102.10, 7102.21 or 7102.31; lab-grown diamonds: 7104.91 or 7104.21. The rate table on the overview page lists all 140 lines.

faqs.question: Do you have to pay customs duty on jewelry you bring into the U.S.?
searchedAs: do you have to pay customs on jewelry
do you have to pay duty on jewelry
can i bring gold jewelry to usa
what is the customs duty on jewelry
faqs.answer: A returning U.S. resident can bring up to $800 of goods bought abroad, jewelry included, duty-free in accompanied baggage (19 CFR 148.33); personal-use baggage is also outside the 2026 Section 301 duty. Above that, or for jewelry shipped or sold, the base rate (5%–13.5% for fine jewelry) plus the country's extra duty applies. Duty-free de minimis entry of parcels under $800 has been suspended since August 29, 2025.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on gold coins?
faqs.answer: No for legal-tender bullion coins such as the Canadian Maple Leaf, Krugerrand or Britannia: they are 7118.90 (Free) and exempt from the Section 301 duty, so they pay nothing from any country — Chinese coin aside (7.5% List 4A). Coin that is not legal tender (7118.10, Free) is not exempt, and from Canada it pays 50% under Section 338. Transporting more than $10,000 in coin must be reported.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on platinum and palladium?
faqs.answer: No. Platinum, palladium, rhodium, iridium, osmium and ruthenium (heading 7110) are Free and exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty, so South African, Swiss or UK platinum pays nothing. Chinese platinum-group metals pay 25% (List 3); Russian ones pay column 2 or 35%. No Section 232 duty applies to them.
